rows.question: How do I change the address on my driving licence?
keyFacts: It does not cost anything to change your address with DVLA
You can apply online (or by post)

answer.answer:
It's free to change your address with DVLA, and you can still drive while you wait for the new licence.

Online (fastest): Sign in to DVLA's online service with GOV.UK sign-in, which may ask you to prove your identity (usually with photo ID such as a passport or driving licence). Apply to change the address on your full or provisional licence. Your licence should arrive within a week. You'll get a confirmation email.

By post: Photocard licence: fill in the "changes" section of letter D741 (included with your licence), then send the licence and the letter to DVLA, Swansea, SA99 1BN, with the correct postage. If you don't have the D741, use form D1 (cars/motorcycles) or D2 (lorries/buses), available from most Post Offices. Paper licence: send a completed D1 or D2, your licence, original documents confirming your identity, and a passport photograph, with the correct postage. Post applications usually take up to 3 weeks.

Also update: your vehicle log book (V5C), your vehicle tax Direct Debit if you pay that way, and your personalised registration number document (V750 or V778) if you have one. You can be fined up to £1,000 if you don't tell DVLA when your address changes.

If you're moving abroad, you can't change the address on a British licence; contact the driving licence authority in your new country. Northern Ireland has a different process.

rows.question: How long do penalty points stay on my licence?
keyFacts: Penalty points/endorsements stay on your driving record for 4 or 11 years, depending on the offence

answer.answer: It depends on the offence. Most penalty points (endorsements) stay on your driving record for 4 years, counted from the date of the offence (or from the date of conviction for some offences, e.g. reckless/dangerous driving or offences resulting in disqualification). Drink and drug driving offences (codes DR10–DR61) and causing death by careless driving while under the influence (CD40, CD50, CD60) or failing to provide a specimen (CD70) stay for 11 years from the date of conviction. For example, a 4-year endorsement for an offence on 10 June 2012 stays until 10 June 2016. An endorsement is 'valid' for the first 3 years (4-year) or 10 years (11-year), and courts can take it into account while valid. Insurers and employers may see it for the whole 4 years, or for the first 5 years of an 11-year endorsement.

rows.question: How do I tell DVLA my car is off the road?
keyFacts: Tell DVLA online (or by phone/post) that the vehicle is off the road: a SORN
You get a refund for any full months of remaining tax

answer.answer:
Tell DVLA your car is off the road by making a SORN (Statutory Off Road Notification). You can do it in three ways:
- Online at gov.uk/make-a-sorn, if the car is registered in your name. You'll need the 11-digit number from your V5C log book or the 16-digit reference from your vehicle tax reminder (V11 letter, email or text).
- By phone: 0300 123 4321 (24-hour service).
- By post: send form V890 to DVLA, Swansea, SA99 1AR. You can apply for this month, or next month or the month after (include a letter explaining why if you're not sending it nearer the time).

Start date: the SORN starts immediately if your vehicle tax has already expired, or if you're not applying in the month the tax is due to expire. If you apply in the month the tax is due to expire, it starts on the first day of the next month.

Other cases: if you have no log book, send a V62 application (a new log book costs £25) with the V890. If the car isn't registered in your name, fill in the appropriate part of the log book and send it with the V890. If you've already sold the car, you don't need a SORN; tell DVLA it's sold instead.

You'll get a refund for any full months of remaining vehicle tax, but you can't use the car on the road until you tax it again.

rows.question: What do I need to do when I sell my car?
keyFacts: Tell DVLA you've sold or transferred the vehicle
You get a refund for any full months of vehicle tax left

answer.answer:
When you sell a car, you need to tell DVLA that you're no longer the registered keeper:

1. Tell DVLA online (the "Tell DVLA you've sold, transferred or bought a vehicle" service, open Monday to Friday 7am to 9pm and Saturday and Sunday 7am to 8pm). You can't use this if you've already posted the log book (V5C) or don't have it. Doing this changes the registered keeper and sends the log book to the new keeper.
2. Your vehicle tax is cancelled after you tell DVLA, and you get a refund for any full months of remaining tax.
3. Give the buyer the log book. If you have the older style V5C, fill in section 6; if you have the newer style with multi-coloured numbered blocks, fill in section 2. Then give the green 'new keeper' slip to the buyer and send the V5C to DVLA.
4. If you sell to a motor trader, they fill in the yellow 'sell, transfer or part-exchange your vehicle to the motor trade' section of the V5C. You send the perforated section to DVLA and give them the rest of the log book.
5. If you don't have the log book, write to DVLA (DVLA, Swansea, SA99 1BA) with your name and address, the registration number, make and model, the exact sale date, and the new keeper's or motor trader's name and address. Make sure you pay the correct postage. Tell the buyer they'll need to apply for a new V5C using form V62 (£25 fee).

The buyer must tax the vehicle before driving it, or declare it off the road (SORN), because tax doesn't transfer to them.

rows.question: What should I do if my car has been stolen?
keyFacts: Tell the police (dial 101) and your insurance company straight away
If the insurer pays out, you must tell DVLA the vehicle has been sold to the insurer

answer.answer:
1. Report it to the police straight away. Call 101, ask for your local police, and have your registration number, make and model, and colour ready. You'll get a crime reference number, which you need for your insurer. The police will tell DVLA about the theft, and will also tell DVLA if the vehicle is found.
2. Tell your insurance company straight away and use the crime reference number to make a claim. They'll explain how to claim.
3. If your insurer pays out, you must tell DVLA the vehicle has been sold to the insurance company. You can do this online or by filling in the yellow 'sell, transfer or part-exchange to the motor trade' section of the log book (V5C) and sending the perforated section to DVLA, with a letter giving the payment date and your insurer's details. Send the rest of the log book to your insurer (if they ask for the whole log book, write to DVLA with your insurer's details, claim date, registration number, make, model, colour and signature, at DVLA, Swansea, SA99 1BD).
4. If you have a private (personalised) registration number you want to keep, apply to keep it as soon as the vehicle is stolen, within 2 years and 6 months of telling DVLA. You can only get it back if you told the police, and the vehicle had a valid MOT and up-to-date vehicle tax when it was stolen. Get the number back before you tell DVLA you no longer own the vehicle.

rows.question: What are the penalties for speeding?
keyFacts: The minimum penalty is a £100 fine and 3 penalty points
You could be disqualified if you reach 12 or more points within 3 years

answer.answer: The minimum penalty for speeding is a £100 fine and 3 penalty points on your licence. If you plead guilty, you pay the fine and get 3 points, unless you're offered a speed awareness course (possible if the police consider it appropriate and you haven't been on one in the past 3 years). If you plead not guilty, you go to court, where the fine is usually a percentage of your weekly income, up to a maximum of £1,000 (£2,500 if on a motorway), and you can get more penalty points and/or be disqualified or have your licence suspended. You can be disqualified if you build up 12 or more penalty points within 3 years. Speeding offences (codes SP10 to SP50) carry 3 to 6 penalty points and stay on your driving record for 4 years from the date of the offence. The police may also give you a verbal warning instead of an FPN or court summons.

rows.question: How do I get my licence back after a driving ban?
keyFacts: You must apply for a new licence to drive again
For drink or drug driving you can reapply before the disqualification ends, using the D27 form DVLA sends

answer.answer:
It depends on the type of ban, but in general you must reapply for a licence before you can drive again once the disqualification ends:

- Check when your ban ends: online via your driving record, on the reminder form D27 (sent 56 days before the end), or on the D27PH letter for some drink-related bans (90 days before). You can also contact DVLA (or DVA in Northern Ireland).
- Disqualified for less than 56 days: you don't need to apply for a new licence; you can drive again once the period has ended.
- Disqualified for 56 days or more (including drink or drug driving): wait for the D27 renewal form (sent 56 days before the end; 90 days for high risk offenders), or get form D1 (car/motorcycle) or D2 (lorry/bus) from a Post Office that offers DVLA services if it doesn't arrive. Fill it in, send it to DVLA with the licence fee (and a passport-style photo if asked). You can apply before the ban ends, but you cannot drive until it has finished.
- If the court said you must retake your driving test, you need a new provisional licence and must pass the tests before driving again. You can drive as soon as the ban is over and the tests are passed.
- If your licence was revoked (cancelled) rather than just disqualified, or you're a new driver whose licence was cancelled within 2 years of passing your test, you must apply for a new provisional licence and retake both parts of the test. Otherwise, you can apply for a new licence at any time using form D1 from the Post Office.
- If you're on a non-GB licence, DVLA will return your licence when the disqualification ends.
- Some drink-drive bans of 12 months or more can be reduced by taking a drink-drive rehabilitation course.

rows.question: Can I drive if I have diabetes?
keyFacts: You must tell DVLA if your insulin treatment lasts (or will last) over 3 months
You do not need to tell DVLA if the diabetes is treated by diet alone

answer.answer:
Yes, in most cases you can drive with diabetes, but you may need to tell DVLA depending on your treatment. For a car or motorbike licence:
- Diet-controlled diabetes: you do not need to tell DVLA.
- Non-insulin medication or diet: check with your doctor or nurse whether you need to tell DVLA. If you do, fill in form DIAB1 (or report online).
- Insulin: you must tell DVLA if your insulin treatment lasts (or will last) over 3 months. This also applies to gestational diabetes if insulin continues more than 3 months after the birth.
- Disabling hypoglycaemia (severe low blood sugar), or a medical professional has told you that you are at risk of it: you must tell DVLA.

For a bus, coach or lorry licence, you do not need to tell DVLA if you are not on insulin. If you start insulin treatment, you must stop driving and tell DVLA, and DVLA will tell you when you can start again.

Failing to tell DVLA about a relevant medical condition can lead to a fine of up to £1,000, and you may be prosecuted if you are involved in an accident as a result.

rows.question: What are the eyesight rules for driving?
keyFacts: You must be able to read a number plate from 20 metres away
Minimum visual acuity of decimal 0.5 (6/12) on the Snellen scale, with glasses or contact lenses if needed

answer.answer:
Car drivers must be able to read a number plate from 20 metres away, using glasses or contact lenses if needed. The minimum standard is a visual acuity of at least decimal 0.5 (6/12) on the Snellen scale, using both eyes together or the better eye if you have sight in one eye only. You must also have an adequate field of vision, which an optician can test. You must wear glasses or contact lenses every time you drive if you need them to meet this standard. You must tell DVLA about any eyesight problem that affects both eyes (or your only eye if you have one eye). Being short or long sighted or colour blind does not need to be reported, and you don't need to report surgery to correct short sight if you meet the standards.

Lorry and bus drivers have stricter rules: visual acuity of at least 0.8 (6/7.5) in the best eye and at least 0.1 (6/60) in the other, with glasses of no more than +8 dioptres or contact lenses. The horizontal visual field must be at least 160 degrees, and any eyesight problem affecting either eye must be reported to DVLA.

You also need to read a number plate on a parked vehicle at the start of your practical driving test, or the test will not continue.

rows.question: What do the codes on my driving licence mean?
keyFacts: The codes on the back of the licence set conditions you must meet to drive
Examples: 01 eyesight correction (glasses or contact lenses); 78 automatic transmission only

answer.answer:
The codes on the back of your photocard licence show the conditions you must meet to drive. Common ones include:

- 01: glasses or contact lenses needed
- 02: hearing or communication aid needed
- 10 to 43: vehicle modifications, such as modified transmission (10), clutch (15), braking (20), accelerator (25), pedal adaptations (31), control layouts (35), steering (40), mirrors (42) or seats (43)
- 44 (with sub-codes 1 to 12): motorbike adaptations
- 45: motorbikes only with a sidecar
- 78 or 106: restricted to automatic vehicles
- 79: restricted to vehicles matching the specification in brackets
- 70: licence exchanged; 71: duplicate licence
- 101: not for hire or reward
- 102: drawbar trailers only
- 103: subject to certificate of competence
- 105: vehicle not more than 5.5 metres long
- 110: limited to transporting persons with restricted mobility
- 115: organ donor
- 96: may drive a vehicle and trailer within the stated weight limits
- 97: cannot drive C1 vehicles that need a tachograph
- 118: start date is for earliest entitlement
- 122: valid on completion of the Basic Moped Training Course

There are other codes for specific vehicle categories and older licences, and some differ in Northern Ireland. The full table is on the GOV.UK page. Codes such as MR, LC or NE99 on your driving record are penalty endorsement codes, not licence conditions.

rows.question: How do I swap my paper driving licence for a photocard?
keyFacts: You do not need to exchange a valid paper licence unless you change your address or name, want to do Driver CPC training, or it is damaged, lost or stolen
It is free if you changed your name or address and still have the paper licence
Otherwise a new photocard licence costs £20

answer.answer:
You only need to swap a paper licence if you change your address or name, want to do Driver CPC training, or your licence is defaced, lost, stolen or destroyed. If none of these apply and your paper licence is still valid, you don't need to exchange it.

If you do need to exchange it:
- Online: sign in to the GOV.UK "renew/exchange" service (you can create sign-in details if needed). You may be asked to prove your identity, usually with photo ID such as a passport or driving licence. To use the online service you must be a resident of Great Britain, not disqualified or prevented from driving for any reason, and meet the minimum eyesight requirement. You cannot apply online if you've changed your name; use the postal route instead.
- By post: fill in form D1 (cars and motorbikes) or form D2 (buses and lorries), available from most Post Offices. Include your original identity documents, a colour passport-type photo, and the fee if required (cheques or postal orders payable to DVLA, no cash). Send ccar and motorbike applications to DVLA, Swansea, SA99 1BU, or bus and lorry applications to DVLA, Swansea, SA99 1BR. Pay the correct postage.

Fees: free if you've changed your name or address and still have your paper licence. £20 if your licence has been defaced, lost, stolen or destroyed, or for any other reason. Online payment is by Mastercard, Visa, Electron or Delta debit or credit card.

Timing: DVLA aims to send the new licence within 3 weeks, possibly longer if your medical or personal details need checking. You may be able to keep driving while it's processed if you meet the conditions on the page (for example, you have your doctor's support and only drive under the conditions of your previous licence). DVLA emails a confirmation once you've applied.

rows.question: How do I tax a car if I haven't received a tax reminder?
keyFacts: You can tax online with the 11-digit reference number from your V5C (or the 12-digit number on the green new keeper slip)
You can also tax by phone or at a Post Office

answer.answer:
You don't need the reminder letter (V11), email or text to tax your car. You can tax it online, by phone, or at a Post Office that deals with vehicle tax.

- Online: you need the 11-digit reference number from your V5C logbook (if you're the current keeper), or the 12-digit reference number from the green new keeper slip (if you've just bought the car and don't have a V5C in your name yet).
- By phone: call DVLA on 0300 123 4321 with your V5C or new keeper slip to hand.
- At a Post Office: take your V5C in your name (or a V62 application if you're the current keeper, or the new keeper slip). You may also need payment and evidence of a current MOT, such as an MOT history screenshot or your MOT certificate. In Northern Ireland you also need a valid MOT certificate and an insurance certificate or cover note.

If you're the current keeper and don't have a V5C, apply for a replacement V5C (£25). You can tax the vehicle at the same time. If you're a new keeper without a V5C or new keeper slip, you can't tax the vehicle until you have a V5C in your name, and you apply for one by post (the form is also available at the Post Office).

You can check online that the vehicle has been taxed.

rows.question: I've just bought a used car. What do I need to do to tax it and get it registered in my name?
keyFacts: You must tax the vehicle before you can use it on the road
The seller usually registers a used vehicle for you, online or by post
You can tax it using the reference number from the green 'new keeper' slip

answer.answer:
1. Tax the car immediately. You can't use a used vehicle on the road until it's taxed. Go to the GOV.UK vehicle tax service and use the green 'new keeper' slip from the log book (V5C) as your reference number. You can pay by Direct Debit or debit/credit card. You must tax it even if it's exempt.

2. Get it registered to you. The seller will usually do this for you, either online or by post:
- Online: the seller registers the vehicle to you online, fills in the green 'new keeper' slip and gives it to you, and destroys the V5C.

rows.question: I'm over 70 and have a medical condition. How do I renew my driving licence?
keyFacts: You can renew online for free from 70 if you meet the eyesight requirement and nothing prevents you from driving
You must tell DVLA about medical conditions that affect your driving

answer.answer:
If you're 70 or over (or will be within 90 days), you renew online with DVLA for free, and you must renew every 3 years. You can use the online service if your licence has expired or will expire within 90 days, you're a resident of Great Britain (Northern Ireland uses a different service), you meet the minimum eyesight requirement, and nothing prevents you from driving. (C1 and D1 entitlements must be renewed by post.)

Your medical condition: you must tell DVLA about any notifiable condition when you renew. You don't need to contact DVLA separately, because the application form asks for this information. Notifiable conditions include things like diabetes (or insulin use), fainting, heart conditions, sleep apnoea, epilepsy, stroke and glaucoma, and anything that could affect your ability to drive safely. Failing to declare can bring a fine of up to £1,000 and prosecution if you have an accident.

After you apply, DVLA may contact your doctor or consultant, arrange an examination, or ask for a driving or eyesight test. This can take longer. They may decide you can keep your licence, give you a shorter licence (1, 2, 3 or 5 years), require adapted controls, or tell you to stop driving. You can usually keep driving while DVLA considers your application, provided you have your doctor's support and meet the other conditions on the official page (for example, your application is less than a year old and your last licence wasn't revoked or refused for medical reasons).

If you're told to stop driving, you can send more medical evidence, reapply when allowed, or appeal (in England and Wales, within 6 months to the magistrates' court; in Scotland, within 21 days to the sheriff's court).

keyFacts: Set it up when you tax your vehicle online or at a Post Office

answer.answer:
You can set up a vehicle tax Direct Debit when you tax your vehicle, either online on GOV.UK or at a Post Office. You don't need to be the registered keeper, but emails and letters about the payments go to the account holder.

You'll need:
- your address and date of birth
- your bank or building society name, account number and sort code

You can't use an account that requires 2 signatures.

You'll get a confirmation by email or post. The first payment is taken once the vehicle tax has started, which can take up to 10 days, and you can keep using the vehicle before it's taken. Later payments are taken on the first working day of the month the Direct Debit is due.

You can pay yearly with no surcharge. Monthly or 6-monthly payments carry a 5% surcharge.
